reason: While the text describes Saul and the men of Israel gathered together in the Valley of Elah preparing for battle against the Philistines, the narrative does not depict genuine collaboration and joint working. Instead, when Goliath challenges them, the people become afraid and dismayed (וַיֵּחַתּוּ וַיִּרְאוּ מְאֹד). The people remain passive and fearful throughout, asking only what reward will be given to whoever defeats the Philistine. David acts as an individual volunteer, not as part of a coordinated collective effort with the leaders or people. While Saul blesses David's individual action, this represents hierarchical approval rather than collaborative partnership. The people ultimately benefit from David's individual victory against Goliath, but they do not actively work together with leadership to achieve it. The text emphasizes individual heroism and divine providence, not collaborative leadership-people dynamics.
